deep.reconstruction:
The page is a numerical table, not a derivation. It is a reduction table for meridian (transit-instrument) observations of eleven bright northern stars, of the kind used to reduce wire transits to the middle wire.

Columns, left to right:
(a) Star name.
(b) Declination δ in degrees, minutes and seconds. The values fit the epoch of about 1853. For example, γ UMa has J2000 δ ≈ +53°41.7'; precessed by about −20"/yr cos α over 147 years this gives ≈ +54°30.7', matching the page.
(c) log cos δ, written in the usual 10-shifted form. Check for α Cygni: cos 44°45'24.27" = 0.710103, whose log is −0.148679, written 9.8513210. I verified this column to within 1 unit of the 7th decimal for α Cyg, α Aur, α Per, η UMa, γ Dra, α Cas, α Cep, β Cep and β UMi.
(d)–(i) Six columns of the form log(i_k · sec δ) = log i_k − log cos δ.

Finding the constants (my reconstruction):
- In every row, (c) + (d) = 11.6171002, so (d) = 1.6171002 − log cos δ.
- The remaining columns differ from (d) by fixed amounts in every row: −0.1652030, −0.4733627, −0.4616005, −0.1537628 and +0.0025653.
- The six constants are therefore log i_k = 1.6171002, 1.4518972, 1.1437375, 1.1554997, 1.4633374, 1.6196655.
- Antilogs: i ≈ 41.410, 28.307, 13.923, 14.305, 29.063, 41.655, which I read as seconds of time.

These are clearly the equatorial wire intervals of a seven-wire transit instrument or meridian circle. They give the distances of wires I, II, III, V, VI, VII from the middle wire IV: about 41.4, 28.3, 13.9 s on one side and 14.3, 29.1, 41.7 s on the other. This is plausibly the Göttingen meridian instrument.

Purpose: a star of declination δ needs i_k sec δ seconds to pass from wire k to the middle wire. Tabulating log(i_k sec δ) lets an observer reduce a transit observed on any wire to the middle-wire time, or combine several wires, or fill in missed wires. This is standard practice (Bessel/Gauss-era reduction of transit observations).

The page uses δ only through sec δ. There is no theory here, only careful 7-place logarithmic computation.
errors: γ Ursae maj.: with δ = 54°30'41.90" as read, log cos δ = 9.7638303, but the table has 9.7638333. This is 3×10⁻⁶ too large, equivalent to about 1.1" in δ; the table value corresponds to δ ≈ 54°30'40.8". Either the seconds are misread (e.g. 40.90 rather than 41.90) or there is a small slip in the source declination or the log lookup. The other columns of this row are internally consistent with 9.7638333.
No other arithmetic errors found. All rows satisfy the constant-sum and constant-difference relations exactly to 7 decimals (checked for β Cep, β UMi, α UMa, α Cyg and others).

results.what: Table of log cos δ and log(i_k sec δ) for 11 northern fundamental stars, with six wire-interval constants i_k ≈ 41.41, 28.31, 13.92, 14.31, 29.06, 41.66 s
results.modern_name: Reduction of transit observations to the middle wire (wire-interval reduction, factor sec δ)
results.usually_credited_to: Standard 18th–19th c. positional astronomy practice (Bradley, Bessel, Gauss; Göttingen and Königsberg observatories)

deep.surprise_reason: This is purely routine astronomical computation: logarithmic sec δ factors for transit-wire reduction. It is mildly interesting biographically, as evidence of Riemann doing or copying observatory reduction work around 1853 in Göttingen, but there is no mathematical novelty.
